title: Aussies continue winning form, Djokovic suffers early exit in Cincinnati
text:
The Australian men's assault at the Cincinnati Open has continued with gusto thanks to Alex de Minaur and Rinky Hijikata.

A day after James Duckworth, Adam Walton and Chris O'Connell scored first-round wins, but Thanasi Kokkinakis was beaten, de Minaur was pushed to his limits at the final Masters 1000 event before the US Open at Flushing Meadows.

Having dropped the first set in just 26 minutes, fifth seed de Minaur, who received an opening-round bye, responded to defeat Quentin Halys 1-6, 6-3, 7-6 (7-4).

The Frenchman had won their only previous meeting, a Miami Masters hard-court clash, back in 2023.

De Minaur lost his opening two service games of the match, but was not broken again en route to setting up a round-of-32 clash with Brit Arthur Fery, who saw off Duckworth, 6-4, 2-6, 7-6, (7-4) in a tick over two-and-a-half hours.

It will be the first clash on tour between de Minaur and the 32nd-seeded French-born Fery.

Earlier on Saturday (Sunday AEST), 25-year-old wildcard Hijikata beat 19th seed Luciano Darderi, of Italy, 6-4, 6-2 to set up his last-32 match with 14th seed Jakub Mensik.

Novak Djokovic was beaten in three sets, by Argentine Thiago Agustin Tirante.

Miomir Kecmanovic, Hubert Hurkacz and Mattia Bellucci were also defeated.

Playing his first match ‌since losing a Wimbledon semifinal to Jannik Sinner, 39-year-old Djokovic struggled in the heat and required a ‌medical timeout in a disappointing US Open tune-up.

"Congrats to my opponent," Djokovic said after losing to the world number 50.

"It was not an enjoyable match for me, for sure. The way I felt. Not the first and I guess not the last time, but it is what it is."

The Serbian — a three-time Cincinnati Open champion and number five in the rankings — will look to regroup before heading to New York, where he ⁠will seek a record-extending 25th grand slam singles ​title.

"I think this is the best win of my career," Tirante said.

"I think I really did a good job inside the court. I managed very well the nerves of playing against a legend like Novak."

ABC/wires

title: Hands On Studio turns 30 as artist hopes Gillard portrait hangs in parliament
text:
Hands On Studio artist Stephen Corsini has big aspirations for his portrait of former prime minister Julia Gillard.

He would like it to be exhibited in Parliament House.

If displayed there, it would not be the first artwork by a Hands On Studio artist to hang on the walls of the iconic Canberra building.

"[To] have this on Parliament House [would be] better than the other one 'cause it's coloured," Mr Corsini said.

The community arts organisation is celebrating its 30th anniversary this weekend, and Mr Corsini has been with it since the beginning.

Mr Corsini said he decided to paint a portrait of Ms Gillard because she had made history by becoming the first female prime minister of Australia.



The painting depicts Ms Gillard in her office in parliament.

"That's the Australian flag there … and that's the Aboriginal flag behind her," Mr Corsini explained.

He said he had deliberately built up the painting layer by layer to make it "stand out".

"I love colour," he said.

"We've made lots of things in the past 30 years."

Hands On Studio is operated by Marymead CatholicCare in Griffith and O'Connor. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

'A flourishing studio'

Hands On Studio has been offering a supported space for people of all abilities to create art since 1996.

Manager and creative director Tilly Davey said it was established by a group of parents for their children who were about to finish school.

Tilly Davey says many artists have been attending the space for decades. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

"The parents worked together and decided to start an arts program, which started in a shed in Curtin and since then has grown into a flourishing studio," she said.

The centre is now operated by Marymead CatholicCare in the M16 Artspace in the Canberra suburbs of Griffith and O'Connor, with 25 art teachers guiding 125 artists each week in painting, textiles, ceramics, stop-motion animation and sculpture.

"We make the rules, they break them and create their own," Ms Davey said.

Hands On Studio artists can attend classes that range from gardening and cooking to creative arts. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

She has been there for 11 years and said it's the best job she's ever had.

"It's kind of like being in a creative vortex. It's just an amazing space," she said.

'Once they start, they don't leave'

Many artists have been attending the studio's classes and workshops for decades, with classes ranging from gardening and cooking to creative arts.

Many artists have been coming back for 15 or 20 years, Ms Davey said, and some, like Mr Orsini, have been attending classes since they began 30 years ago.

"A lot of our artists, once they start, they don't leave."

Some Hands On Studio classes are so popular they have years-long waiting lists. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

The popularity of some classes has led to lengthy waiting lists.

"Quite often I have to tell people, once you're on our waiting list, you may be waiting for 20 years or so, if it's a particular class you want to come to," Ms Davey said.

She attributes the space's popularity to its special ability to give the artists a sense of freedom and ability to express themselves.

"The space is a really important space, not just for the art, but for our artists to feel free and to have a sense of freedom and to be able to be who they are," she said.

Earlier this year, Hands On Studio curated a special exhibit at Canberra Contemporary and is gearing up for shows at Goulburn Regional Art Gallery and Canberra Art Biennial later this year.

Hands On Studio receives the majority of its funding from the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS). (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Studio turns to fundraising amid funding challenges

Hands On Studio relies on the funding its participants receive through the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS), which helps cover the costs of staff and materials.

"All of our artists have NDIS packages. So it is crucial that the artists remain on their NDIS packages to continue to come to programs like this and to support them," Ms Davey said.

Hands On Studio's anniversary celebration will also raise funds, with artwork and other items for sale. (ABC News: Simon Beardsell)

Ms Davey said there were challenges in keeping the program funded and the organisation was turning to fundraising.

"We are working really hard behind the scenes to ensure that our program survives," she said.

This weekend the studio is hosting a celebration and fundraiser to mark 30 years of operations, with artworks and other items for sale.

"I suppose this is our dip into fundraising to see how that goes and also to see what we can do with fundraising and how we can continue to operate," Ms Davey said.

She said there would be a "riot" if the studio were to ever close.

"I can manage an art studio, but I don't know if I can control a riot," she said.

title: Tupou has his 'mojo' back and Wallabies want more
text:
Les Kiss will continue to assure Taniela Tupou's new French bosses the Wallabies are looking after him, thrilled the prop has rediscovered his "mojo" in the Test arena.

Tupou scored two first-half tries for Australia, who trailed before scoring 42 consecutive points in a 56-17 defeat of Japan in Townsville on Saturday.

All three starting front-rowers, as well as replacement hooker Brandon Paenga-Amosa and back-rowers Harry Wilson and Charlie Cale, were Australia's try-scorers in Townsville.

Tupou scored the match-winner in Osaka against Eddie Jones's men a week earlier after coming off the bench and has shown power and skill to indicate he is back near his best approaching next year's home Rugby World Cup.

Wallaby 1,000 has 'dream come true' as Australia thrash Japan Massimo De Lutiis enjoys a dream debut for Australia, scoring a try in his country's commanding 56-17 win over Japan in the second Test.

"He's found a little bit of himself again, and he's been more of himself," Wallabies coach Kiss said, while also noting his combination with good mate and returning lock Lukhan Salakaia-Loto.

"I'm very, very big on making sure the players be themselves as much as possible."

Former Queensland Reds star Tupou agonised over his move from Australian rugby to France, with Racing 92 last season but it has helped him turn back the clock after several underwhelming seasons at the Melbourne Rebels and NSW Waratahs.

"Moving to France, he's found out who he is a little bit more and he's come back and he's really connected with the group here and found that bit of mojo that he likes to thrive on," Kiss said.

With English-based Tom Hooper yet to return to the side, Tupou is the only overseas-based Wallaby currently in the Test rotation.

The coach has remained in touch with Racing 92's staff to ensure they have his services for the two-Test tour of Argentina that begins later this month and hopefully beyond.

"All good, as I believe, at this stage," Kiss said.

"I'll be talking to the coach and the team manager of Racing, this week, again, to make sure they understand how we're looking after Nella and making sure we're doing the right thing with him and working him hard.

"So they can trust the process as well. But, yeah, he'll be with us."

Jones joked post-game that Tupou played as if there was a pizza on offer for every try and reckoned he would even deliver one to the change rooms himself.

"No pizza, I'll have to hit him up about that one," Tupou grinned.

"I've got a lot of love and respect for Eddie, actually. Nothing against that, he loves me, I know that."

Tupou said he wanted to "take it to the next level" after finding his feet in France.

And he said Kiss's tweaks were helping him get there.

"To get the ball in my hands as a forward, less running without the ball, more running with it," Tupou said.

"We're still working on it, but it's good to see forwards scoring tries."

AAP

title: Menopause and music: pioneer women's health doctor dies at 94
text:
Dr Margaret Smith was fond of describing herself as "not famous, but well-known".

The renowned Perth obstetrician and women's health advocate delivered some 6,000 babies throughout a decades-long career, during which she had to battle the sexism rampant in the male-dominated hierarchies of medicine in the 1950s and beyond.

Dr Smith died on July 14, her 94th birthday.

In his eulogy, family friend Julian Dowse said she often paraphrased the famous quote that described golden-age Hollywood actors Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire dancing together.

"I have to do everything he does backwards and in high heels, but fortunately I can make it look twice as easy," Mr Dowse quoted her as saying.

Margie, as she was often called, was a twin, born four minutes before her identical sister Joan.

Their mother, attended by just a midwife and expecting a single baby, had picked out one girl's name: 'Margaret Joan'. Such was the shock at the multiple birth that the girls were only given one name each. Their sister Nancy completed the family four years later.

Margaret and her sister Joan were so alike they were sometimes referred to as `Margaretorjoan’ by schoolmates (Supplied)

As a child, she became determined to pursue a medical career when a favourite cousin died in her teens in the era before antibiotics. Later her grandmother's death from ovarian cancer steered her towards women's health.

No residencies for women

Margie graduated from the University of Adelaide in 1956, one of only four women in her class of more than 100 men.

Initially, she was refused a residency in obstetrics because she was female.

Mr Dowse said her classmates made sure she got what she wanted.

"There was a famous act of solidarity by her fellow students, who refused to take up their residencies unless the talented Margie was offered a rightful place," he said.

Loading...

The lead campaigner was Frank Smith, who was to become Margie's husband. The couple had no children.

"Margie once said to me, reflecting on the dilemmas that professional women of her era faced:

'I could not have had children, otherwise I could not have done what I did for other children'," Mr Dowse said.

A pioneer in women's health

Margie spent five years training as a specialist in Edinburgh, winning a gold medal in her postgraduate examinations in 1963 for the highest-performing student in the realm.

In the 1970s, she and Frank spent seven years in the highlands of Papua New Guinea, where Frank worked as a surgeon, and Margie delivered babies.

But her role in the remote location went far beyond obstetrics, and she was often a physician and anaesthetist, practising in difficult circumstances without the support of specialist teams.

"During this time, Margie was most proud of safely delivering a set of triplets," Mr Dowse said.

Margaret Smith delivered about 6,000 babies during her long career. (Supplied)

After Papua New Guinea, the couple moved to Perth, where Margie was one of the few female practitioners at the time. She worked both at King Edward Memorial Hospital and in private practice, as well as lecturing at the University of Western Australia.

"Margie revolutionised the treatment and care of women," Mr Dowse said. "She put women first from birth to menopause."

Treating the silent suffering

In the 1970s, menopause was rarely discussed in public but Margie recognised the challenges faced by many women in midlife.

She founded WA's first menopause clinic in 1978, later named in her honour. She was also a founding member of the Australasian Menopause Society.

Colleague Dale Hamilton said she was passionate about teaching women to take better care of their own health.

"She ran a lot of public seminars for education about the menopause and … she was a very clear and passionate speaker, and very, very popular," she said.

" She had a good sense of humour, she was clear about the information, so she imparted a lot of power to women by educating them on what was possible. "

Community recognition

Margie was named a WA Citizen of the Year in 1994, and was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia in 1996 for service to medicine and women's health care.

Dr Margaret Smith working at her desk in 2010. (ABC News)

In 2011, she was inducted into the WA Women's Hall of Fame.

Margie also wrote several books, including a memoir, as well as more than 30 published medical papers.

Throughout her career, she mentored countless young doctors, inspired many colleagues and assisted thousands of patients, all with patience, encouragement and humility.

"Her work was the Hippocratic Oath writ large," Mr Dowse said.

"She safely brought life into the world and sought to make life better for countless others."

Music and medicine

Margie loved classical music, and was a choral singer well into her 90s.

Margaret Smith loved music and poetry (Supplied)

She also loved poetry, and considered Norton's Anthology of Poetry an "indispensable reference book", Mr Dowse said.

"She introduced me to Keats's observation that 'a thing of beauty is a joy forever'," he said.

Late in life, Margie learnt to play the cello and to paint.

"She had a wonderful energy ... no matter what was going on," Dr Hamilton said.

Margie is survived by her twin sister Joan, nieces and nephews, as well as more than one generation of deeply grateful women.

title: Memory of late partner blooms in sharing wildflowers
text:
Leonie Aspin travels from New Zealand to Western Australia's Mid West each year as a kaleidoscope of colourful blooms emerges after winter rains.

For months, she volunteers as a wildflower tour guide in Morawa, 360 kilometres north-east of Perth, in memory of her late partner, Ray Fraser, a former shearer who died from brain cancer in 2022.

A variety of blooms have emerged near Morawa. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

It was Mr Fraser who taught her about wildflowers during long drives around the region.

"[Ray] would sometimes in the morning say, 'Do you want to go hunting for orchids?' and it was just like, 'Yes please,'" Ms Aspin said.

"He was just the best in that aspect."

Leonie Aspin and Ray Fraser would often hunt for orchids together. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Grief-stricken, Ms Aspin moved to New Zealand after Mr Fraser's death, before the lure of wildflowers brought her back.

"It got to a point where I just missed the wildflowers, and it got to the point where I had to test my little heart again," she said.

Ms Aspin now returns each year to continue their shared hobby, guiding tourists to carpets of blooms and pointing out the more understated, hidden gems.

"I know he'll never be there again, but it just helps fill that little empty hole in my heart," she said.

Loading...

Ms Aspin draws parallels between her grief and the seasonal blooms.

"We all have to get off the boat at some time, don't we? And just like wildflowers, well, it's a complete circle of life," she said.

"To see the red dirt transform after the rains into absolute colour; you can't explain it, you need to see it."

Red dirt is hidden under a carpet of wildflowers. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Business behind the blooms

Ms Aspin said tourists were starting to flock to the Mid West.

"It's starting to amp up now, so it will only get busier, so the next month will be absolutely probably crazy," she said.

She said the annual influx was an important boost for the small communities scattered across the wildflower region.

"People are going to need food, coffees, accommodation, obviously fuel," she said.

"It just benefits the whole town."

Tom Pilkington travels every year to see wildflowers. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Tom Pilkington travels from Perth annually to see WA's wildflowers, this year making the four-hour journey to Morawa.

He said the hospitality of the small town was a real drawcard, along with the abundance of blooms.

Some visitors travel to see small, elusive orchids. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"It's a lovely little place … everybody's really friendly and helpful," he said.

"They're just over the moon with giving you information [about] which way to go."

'Other-worldly' scenes

Carla Read and Ray Hatton also travelled from Perth, camping in Morawa while on a five-day journey to Lake Ballard.

The pair said they had not done much wildflower touring before, but were considering making it an annual tradition.

Ray Hatton and Carla Read say they hope to travel during wildflower season again. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"I never used to understand the gold and green thing, and now driving here, I fully get it because everything is gold and green," Ms Read said.

"Being in nature and seeing the flowers … it just takes you somewhere else out of who you normally relate to being.

"It's just other-worldly really.

"It's just that nature. The colour, freedom, the open skies, it's just beautiful, and the red dirt. I love that."

Pink everlastings draw tourists to the Midwest. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chloe Henville)

title: Teen obliterates men's world record in 1,500m freestyle first
text:
The world record for the men's 1,500m freestyle, an event once dominated by Australians Grant Hackett and Kieren Perkins, has been obliterated by 19-year-old German star Johannes Liebmann.

The teenager smashed the record at the European Aquatics Championships in France on Saturday, knocking almost four seconds off the previous record in a dominant display.

The new world-best mark of 14 minutes 26.79 seconds eclipsed the previous record set by American Bobby Finke at the Paris Olympics two years ago by 3.88 seconds. He also became the first man to complete the distance in under 14 minutes 30 seconds.

"I'm just amazed, the time is incredible. I didn't think it was possible for me … I'm just speechless," Liebmann told Olympics.com.

"The race was hard. I started fast, it was planned to just get rid of the others to swim my own race. Halfway through the race, I saw I was way ahead of the others, and I felt good … I guess in the last 200 or 300 metres, I saw the crowd standing up and it just gave me another burst of power."

The teenager said he knew he was going to post a good time, but he had no idea how fast he was going.

"When I saw the crowd standing, I knew probably a European record, maybe a world record, but I thought it was close, so I was a bit overthinking it, and the last 100 metres were so hard, but then just seeing the 14:26 is incredible."

Saturday also saw another world record fall as American Kate Douglass reclaimed the women's 50 metres freestyle world record by registering a time of 23.49 seconds in the preliminaries at the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in Irvine, California.

Reuters/ABC

title: Experts warn H5N1 bird flu spread to the Northern Territory 'inevitable'
text:
Veterinary authorities say it is "inevitable" H5N1 bird flu will spread to the Northern Territory, almost two months after the first case of the disease was identified in Australia.

The virus, first detected in Western Australia in late June, has now been found in all six states, leading to bird vaccination programs in some of them.

Senior Director of Species Management at the NT Department of Lands, Planning and Environment Tony Griffiths said the disease's arrival in the territory was imminent.

Tony Griffiths says it's only a matter of time before the H5N1 bird flu strain arrives in the NT. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"It's definitely going to happen," he said.

" It could be weeks, it could be months, but it's a national event, it's the biggest national disease event that has ever occurred in Australia for wildlife. "

For bird owners like Darwin local "Datto", who frequents Nightcliff Jetty with his galah Buddy, the threat of the flu has created a looming sense of anxiety.

The NT is home to 450 species of bird, 37 of which are considered threatened. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"It's going to take away a lot of privileges of me taking [Buddy] where the other birds are, and we're going to lose a lot of good birds over it," he said.

Datto said an outbreak in Darwin's northern suburbs, where wild birds routinely flock along the coastline, would devastate locals who come to enjoy the wildlife.

"We get all myriads of birds here — the firebirds, the honey eaters and everything else — and it'll be a shame to see all of them in a little pile of feathers on the side of the road," he said.

The NT's Chief Veterinary Officer Sue Fitzpatrick said it was not just wild species that were at risk, urging backyard poultry farmers and other bird owners to be vigilant against the disease.

Sue Fitzpatrick says the Territory's backyard poultry owners can do their bit to help stop the spread of bird flu. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"While we don't have a commercial poultry industry, we certainly have many backyard poultry owners," she said.

"We're looking for bird keepers to protect their birds from wild birds, enclose their runs and put some roof over their runs, protect feed and water sources from wild birds."

Birdwatchers essential to response

Dr Griffiths said the plan to combat H5N1 in the NT would largely rely on wide-scale surveying of areas where birds are known to flock, such as the Top End coastline and Barkly Lakes.

He said while experts had been rigorously sampling faeces and water supplies to identify contamination, vaccination of native species was not on the cards.

The masked lapwing has small spurs on its wings which it uses to protect its chicks. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"We have 450 species of bird in the territory and 37 of those are threatened, but we don't rely on captive breeding programs to support the management of those species," he said.

"The threatened birds we have are dispersed over very large areas and it's very difficult to catch them to vaccinate."

With a vast network of birdwatchers across the NT, Dr Griffiths said the government was looking to harness the power of the territory's avian enthusiasts to tackle the tyranny of distance.

Keen birdwatchers are being urged to use their skills to help monitor the spread of bird flu in the NT. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Biodiversity Watch NT's Graeme Sawyer said having boots on the ground would be essential to the mitigation effort.

"The authorities' problem is always that they haven't got any staff in most places," he said.

" By using bird-watching fraternities, Indigenous communities and ranger programs, you've got people right across the country, and a lot of them know a heck of a lot about their birds. "

Mr Sawyer said anyone with a passion for birds and wildlife conservation could help to slow the spread of the virus.

Graeme Sawyer says the NT's bird-watching fraternities, Indigenous communities and rangers "know a heck of a lot about their birds". (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"I would just urge anybody who's got a remote interest in birds to sharpen up their eyes and get their binoculars out," he said.

"It is a big unknown and the more information we can get early, the better."

title: Socceroo seals mega-money move with Michael Jackson dance
text:
Nestory Irankunda has officially sealed his money-spinning transfer to Portuguese giants Sporting CP, and celebrated the move by starring in a spectacular Michael Jackson-themed dance video.

Sporting CP announced the move from English Championship club Watford on Saturday, with the undisclosed fee reported to be in the region of $26 million and potentially rising with add-ons to $29.5 million.

Loading Instagram content

Ending a week in which teen defender Lucas Herrington became the most expensive Australian footballer of all as he joined Premier League Hull from MLS side Colorado Rapids for a reported package worth $33 million, Irankunda's move was another red-letter day for Aussie soccer.

Sporting CP, the 21-time champions from the capital Lisbon, were certainly making a song and dance of the signing of the youngster who lit up the World Cup for the Socceroos, as they revealed they have inserted a whopping $130 million release clause into Irankunda's contract.

They also greeted the 20-year-old Australian with one of the most innovative welcome videos seen in European football.

To the strains of Michael Jackson's Bad amid Wanted posters, Irankunda stepped out of a sports car and reprised his Jacko-themed goal celebration before metamorphosing into the famous green-and-white hoops.

Sporting CP, which once nurtured the talent of another young winger called Cristiano Ronaldo, clearly think a lot of Irankunda, snapping him up in a five-year deal through to 2031, even though he is yet to truly establish himself at a European club, either in Germany or England.

Negotiations over the sale were complicated because Bayern Munich, who sold Irankunda to Watford, will also get a share of the sell-on. The German giants are expected to garner nearly $10 million from the move.

Irankunda made no bones about his delight at joining a club that can offer him Champions League football this season, after an up-and-down spell at Watford where the highs were soaring with four spectacular goals.

"It's a moment of great happiness and pride," he told the club's fans. "I'm very excited.

"Any child or person who loves football dreams of playing in the UEFA Champions League. Having this opportunity will be fantastic and a dream come true.

"The project seemed very good to me and, obviously, Sporting CP is a top club with a great history. I wanted to accept this challenge and I'm ready.

"Even someone who lives on the other side of the world, like me, looks at Sporting CP and understands how fantastic and passionate the fans are.

"That's why, and also because of the club's history, I get goosebumps thinking that I'm wanted by a club like that.

"When they told me about Sporting CP, it was Sporting CP all the way.

"I came here to win titles and to play for great fans. I want to make history and there's no better place to do that than Sporting CP. I'm very happy to be here and I hope to win trophies this season."

Sporting CP, who nailed down their Champions League place by finishing second behind Porto last year, have already begun their season, picking up their opening Primeira Liga win on Friday with a 3-2 win over Vitoria to move top.

Australian players have been in demand since the Socceroos reached the last-32 at the World Cup.

title: Pacific Airshow brings jet suits, stunts and space pioneers to Gold Coast
text:
Gold Coast pilot Emma McDonald may have a fear of heights, but she never feels more at home than when she's spinning through the sky in an aeroplane.

"If you stick me on top of a building without a rail, unless I've got wings strapped to me — that's actually my little secret," she said.

Emma McDonald is the only female performer at the Pacific Airshow. (Supplied: Pacific Airshow)

Travelling up to 400 kilometres per hour, at an acceleration 10 times the normal force of gravity (or 10Gs), Ms McDonald is one of the best stunt pilots in the industry.

She loves to flip aeroplanes end over end, fly into a vertical position and upside down for fun.

"I grew up in a family of pilots, so we'll have to blame my dad, he was an aerobatic display pilot as well," she said.

Emma McDonald is one of the best stunt pilots in the industry. (Supplied: Pacific Airshow)

Ms McDonald is the only woman to show off her skills at this year's Pacific Airshow, which has returned to the Gold Coast this weekend after a year-long hiatus.

"Being the only one out there, I hope to inspire more girls to have a go," she said.

" Don't let anything hold you back. "

Huge crowds attended this year's air show. (Supplied: Pacific Airshow)

Jet suits make first appearance at show

The international event, which bills itself as Australia's largest air show, also featured its first jet suit demonstration, with two pilots flying and spinning over the ocean, powered by small engines mounted on their backs and arms.

Paul Jones, pilot and lead flight instructor at the UK-based Gravity Industries, said it was "surreal" to soar through the air with crowds watching.

Loading...

"It's mega to be here on the Gold Coast," he said.

"We've been trying to do this for a couple of years and fortunately, we've been able to make it happen."

Paul Jones is a pilot and lead flight instructor at the UK-based Gravity Industries. (ABC Gold Coast: Glenn Mullane)

The jet suits were just one feature of the daily six-hour air show that streaked through the Surfers Paradise sky from Friday to Sunday.

Flight Lieutenant Dave Burnard from the Royal Australian Air Force's aerobatic display team, The Roulettes, said the nerves could be "pretty high" during a routine.

RAAF flight lieutenants Dave Burnard and James Dutschke. (ABC Gold Coast: Glenn Mullane)

"But once you get used to it and you've done a few, it just becomes good old-fashioned fun," he said.

"I really enjoy it, sitting there and singing to myself … sing a bit of Creed, sing a bit of Oasis, whatever the vibe is of the day."

The RAAF Roulettes travelled from their base in eastern Victoria to take part in the show. (Supplied: Pacific Airshow)

Maverick and Rooster make appearances

Even Top Gun impersonators Pete "Maverick" Mitchell and Bradley "Rooster" Bradshaw made an appearance.

"It's fantastic to be here," Maverick told the ABC.

"We fly the F-14, the F-18 for Rooster right here, but here we're going to be doing ground entertainment, mainly."

Impersonators of Top Gun's Rooster and Maverick made an appearance. (ABC News)

Asked if they could give the performing pilots a run for their money: "That's classified," Maverick said.

"We'd tell you but we'd have to kill you."

This year's air show featured a rare two-seater version of the WWII Supermarine Spitfire. (Supplied: Pacific Airshow)

Australian astronaut inspiring next generation

Ms McDonald is not the only woman breaking down barriers at this year's event.

Katherine Bennell-Pegg, the first astronaut to formally represent Australia, also attended the event and spoke to about 5,000 school students.

Katherine Bennell-Pegg is the first astronaut to formally represent Australia. (ABC Gold Coast: Glenn Mullane)

"I'm excited to pass onto them that energy and that knowledge that they can do more than they imagine," she said.

"They can be the ones flying those planes in the sky, they can be the ones designing and building them, they can aspire to one day be an astronaut."

While she hasn't yet flown to space, Ms Bennell-Pegg said the European Space Agency had made an offer to the Australian government for a potential mission.

"For me now, my focus is on remaining match-fit for space, should I have that opportunity," she said.

title: Gardening is about more than food for young people learning English
text:
For the first time since he left Africa, 16-year-old Albert Lotemo is delighted to have his hands in the dirt.

Born in the Democratic Republic of Congo and raised in Zambia, he would work every day on a bountiful harvest as part of his agriculture studies.

Loading...

"I was planting the food like maize, cassava … some orange, banana … and lemon and pineapple," he said.

" Actually, I'm feeling good because today is my first time in Australia doing another garden … like in school in Zambia. "

Albert has been studying for six months at Blackburn English Language School's (BELS) Wodonga campus in north-east Victoria.

BELS acts as a bridge for young migrants and refugees with limited English to transition to mainstream schools.

The students will soon plant vegetables including spring onion, lettuce, and carrots. (Supplied: Headspace)

The school has partnered with youth mental health organisation Headspace, under local organisation Gateway Health, to plant the seeds of a new garden to assist the students with some of the challenges of living in a new country.

Growing connections

Refugees are at higher risk of poor mental health but less likely to seek help, according to the Australian Institute of Family Studies.

What do you want to tell us? Have Your Say Our best stories start with listening to yours. Tell us what Australia should know.

Possible barriers include a lack of understanding or trust in the new healthcare system, stigma around mental illness, and limited finances, language skills or transport.

The BELS garden project aims to help young people escape social isolation and forge ties to their new community.

"Gardening is a way for those students to connect and it doesn't rely solely on their English skills," local Headspace cultural connections coordinator Ruby Huang said.

Ruby Huang says the garden will lead to cooking classes. (ABC News: Alice Walker)

"It provides a safe space for our young people to share their traditions, their knowledge … working together," she said.

She hopes the project will blossom into a pathway from paddock to plate.

Students will also bring seedlings from home to share their food culture. (ABC News: Alice Walker)

"The idea is for them to grow what they eat and eat what they grow," she said.

"Imagine that one day they bring produce from the garden back home for their parents to cook — that'd be so, so exciting."

Mental oxygen

Albert is not the only student to hold fond memories of food production.

"Something that all our newly arrived students can really connect with is gardening," said science teacher Regina Glass.

Regina Glass is shaping her sustainability lessons around the garden. (ABC News: Alice Walker)

"There's a number of community gardens in the Wodonga area that are primarily run by migrants."

The school's 21 students from Congolese, Vietnamese, Nepalese and Indian backgrounds will use the garden as part of their science curriculum.

Ms Glass said the project provided cognitive breathing space for children overloaded with the demands of learning a new language.

Regina Glass with students Ornela Mulerwa (left) and Georgette Byaombe Alphonse (middle). (ABC News: Alice Walker)

"Anyone who has been overseas to somewhere where they don't speak the language will know how tired people are after a day of trying to navigate the world in a different language," she said.

"It's not like sitting in a class just being talked at."

For young Albert, it has also opened up dreams for the future.

"When I have my own money, I can have my own farm and I can work in the garden," he said.

title: Key Demon faces nervous MRO wait with AFL finals near after high shot
text:
Melbourne forward Jacob van Rooyen faces a nervous match review officer (MRO) wait after collecting a "flat" Aliir Aliir during the Demons' commanding 20.12 (132) to 8.8 (56) win over Port Adelaide.

Despite the win keeping the surging Demons in the hunt for a top four finish, the big talking point from Saturday's clash at Adelaide Oval was the hit from van Rooyen, with the Demons spearhead set to face MRO scrutiny with the finals just a few weeks away.

The Melbourne forward was attempting to spoil an Aliir mark in the second term, but appeared to mistime it and struck the Power defender high with a swinging arm.

Aliir, who went down and had to be helped off the field by trainers, failed his HIA test and spent the rest of his milestone 200th AFL game watching from the bench.

"He's OK," Power coach Josh Carr said of Aliir post-game.

"Obviously, he's a little bit flat and a bit quiet, but Aliir is a leader. He'll find a way to get himself up.

"Look, this is honest truth. I haven't looked at it closely, but my first thought of it is I can see how it happens.

"It obviously didn't look great, but I didn't think it was overly malice either."

Demons coach Steven King, who said he "hadn't really seen" the incident, added it was "really unfortunate" for the Power intercept defender.

Melbourne will finish the weekend fifth on the ladder, level on points with Brisbane (third) and Hawthorn (fourth) but with a worse percentage.

The Demons host Western Bulldogs in the final home-and-away game next weekend, needing a win to guarantee they finish in the top-six and bypass the wildcard round and go straight to finals.

title: Hobbies light up life for older people transitioning to retirement
text:
For more than 50 years, Annie Delaine cared for communities across Australia.

From working in the Torres Strait Islands as a remote-area nurse to managing operating rooms in regional South Australia, not a day went by when she did not love the work she was doing.

"I worked in the islands for 16 years … you did everything, from delivering babies, immunising children to looking after their parents," she said.

"You were looking after the entire health of the islands, and I just loved it."

The people and community connections are what stopped Annie Delaine (right) from wanting to retire. (Supplied: Annie Delaine)

As Ms Delaine approached her retirement years, she began to struggle with the idea of her next chapter.

"It took me four times to retire before I bit the bullet and did it," she said.

"I deregistered just so I wouldn't go back.

"When I did, I thought to myself, 'How am I going to fill in the gap?' Because it was a big one to fill."

Annie Delaine had bought paint years before but gave it to island locals instead. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Nudging 70 and retiring for a fourth time, she tried her hand at art, a passion she secretly had for years but was too afraid to try.

"My husband bought me the biggest canvas, and I nearly had a heart attack," she laughed.

"For a year, it sat behind the spare bedroom door, until one day I got brave and pulled it out.

"Painting is now my happy place. I can lose hours and hours and then realise the sun is going down."

Annie Delaine's husband helped create an art room in their house. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Two years since picking up the paintbrush, Ms Delaine now has a dedicated art room inside her home and has found her retirement passion.

It is a journey she is encouraging others to follow, in an effort to reframe what retirement can look like for the everyday Australian.

Retirement planning importance

Loneliness is a common experience for many hanging up their work boots.

University of Sydney public health professor Melody Ding has found through her research that human connections should be prioritised just as much as financial planning.

"Loneliness, especially sustained periods, could potentially cause long-term health impacts, including early mortality," she said.

"If we retire with plenty of money but no health, no friends and no social network … we're really missing a bigger picture.

Melody Ding says community connection is important for a healthy retirement. (ABC News: Patrick Thomas)

"Good supportive social networks are equally important as other aspects of healthy lifestyles, such as eating healthy and being physically active."

Professor Ding said it was not uncommon for people to struggle to retire due to identity loss.

She said the earlier you could start planning for retirement, the better your life could be.

"When we stop working, we often lose that sense of purpose, so finding another identity and community is really critical to our happiness post-retirement," she said.

"Even though retirement is far away [for some], it is important to start thinking about how we can preserve our health and positive social relationships, because all of it takes investment."

Art participation on the rise

Participation in visual arts and craft events among Australians aged over 50 increased by 7 per cent between 2022 and 2025, according to Creative Australia's national arts survey.

More than 30 people are enrolled in an art class for people aged over 50 in SA's Riverland. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

U3A is a worldwide volunteer-run organisation that offers activities designed for older people entering retirement who want to keep their minds and bodies active.

In South Australia's Riverland, more than 20 participants partake in the Berri branch U3A art classes each week.

Kate Yates says getting out of your comfort zone is great for wellbeing. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Kate Yates is one of three art tutors and said it had been fantastic to see participants' confidence grow.

"Putting ourselves out of our comfort zone is very good for us, even if we don't think it at the time," she said.

"Gardening is great, but it is solitary; here [at the art classes], you have to keep mingling and meeting new people."

John Selfe says art classes have changed his life. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Class participant John Selfe moved to Renmark three years ago and said he experienced immense loneliness for more than a year.

That was until his sister dragged him along to the local art class.

"I started off very nervous, thinking, 'Am I going to make a fool of myself?' But you just let your pencil do the talking," he said.

"It just lights up your life … [sometimes] I think about the wasted years I wasn't doing art, but hey, it's not over till it's over."

Never too late to do what you love

Since creating colourful canvases, Ms Delaine is now exhibiting her work as part of the South Australian Living Artists Festival (SALA) alongside seven other local women.

She said her journey should serve as a lesson to anyone that it is never too late to learn a new skill and find a new passion.

Annie Delaine's dog Suki is named after Suki Village in Papua New Guinea, where she spent time nursing. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

"Just through art, I have met so many people I would not have known before and that's good," she said

"It doesn't matter what you go into, as long as you give it a go.

"Retired, I'm not sure I like the name; I prefer to think of it as having fun once you've finished work."

title: Memory lapses, fake invoices and a reprimand: Key moments from ICAC
text:
Fake invoices, a "stupid joke" and a reprimand in the hearing room — it has been another revealing week at NSW's corruption watchdog.

The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is examining allegations involving illegal political donations and whether people linked to fugitive property developer Jean Nassif sought to influence political and government outcomes.



Operation Rosny has almost hit the halfway mark.

Here is a look back at the key moments from the week and what is coming next.

'Don't give me that look'

Lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood spent three days in the ICAC witness box, and it is not the last the commission will see from him.

Mr Greenwood often made the job of counsel assisting a struggle, with repeated answers of "I don't know" and "I don't recall" when asked about key events or conversations.

At one stage, he said he could not remember details from a phone call he had that morning.

Mr Greenwood often responded to questions with "I don't know", and "I don't recall". (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

There were several tense exchanges and, at one point, Mr Greenwood snapped, saying to someone in the room: "Don't give me that look."

It is not clear who the 37-year-old was referring to, but the outburst earned him a scolding from Commissioner Fabian Gleeson SC, who reminded him to listen to questions and maintain respectful conduct and "decorum".

He was also pressed about a text exchange that emerged earlier in the inquiry, when he told lobbyist Jean-Claude Perrottet he had given him "filthy schools money" and had put up with his "f***ing whinging".

When asked about it, Mr Greenwood chalked it up to a "stupid joke" between friends, saying he was trying to rile Mr Perrottet.

But Counsel Assisting Peggy Dwyer SC put it to him that the "filthy schools money" referred to Catholic Schools NSW (CSNSW) funds allegedly being funnelled into Liberal Party recruitment.

There were tense exchanges between Mr Greenwood and Dr Dwyer this week. (Supplied: ICAC)

Mr Greenwood also said he could not recall what work his lobbying firm, Beckington, was doing for its client, Dallas McInerney, despite being paid $6,000 a month by the then-CSNSW CEO.

The commission has heard Mr Greenwood and his former business partner Christian Ellis allegedly used Beckington to issue "sham" invoices disguising prohibited political donations.

Monthly donations questioned

Mr McInerney, spent two days in the ICAC witness box this week, as one of the key figures in the inquiry.

He stood aside from the role after he was named in the ICAC's investigation.

As anticipated, he faced a barrage of questions over his dealings with federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, who was named earlier in the probe.

In the first week of hearings, the commission was shown a message Mr McInerney sent to NSW Reformers co-founder Robert Assaf about Mr Taylor, in which he declared: "I want to shake down Angus for 10k."

Mr McInerney gave evidence over two days and is due to return next week. (ABC News)

Another message, from former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw, claimed Mr McInerney secured a $15,000 payment from Mr Taylor, and ongoing monthly donations of $3,000 for the Reformers' work.

Mr McInerney acknowledged seeking financial support from Mr Taylor but insisted it had nothing to do with the right-wing Liberal faction group, the NSW Reformers, a group at the centre of the inquiry.

He said it was instead intended to support NSW Liberal internal elections and conservative candidates in key seats.

Mr Taylor denied making any payment and is not accused of wrongdoing.

Who's up next at inquiry?

Mr McInerney is expected to appear again on Wednesday before former Liberal minister David Elliott takes the stand.

The ICAC is also examining whether donations linked to Mr Nassif were exchanged for political favours, including attempts to damage Mr Elliott's career.

It previously heard NSW Liberal Party operatives allegedly compiled a "David Elliott shit sheet" — a dossier of political and personal allegations aimed at damaging his career.

Mr Elliott is due to give evidence mid next week. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

Mr Whitelaw also told the commission Mr Greenwood and Mr Ellis claimed to have photographs of Mr Elliott involved in an alleged extramarital affair, although he was never shown them and accepted it may never have occurred.

Mr Greenwood said he commissioned the document to defend his business interests, rather than target Mr Elliott politically.

He also said he did not believe the allegation of an affair was true and said he received a photograph of Mr Elliott arriving home that he intended to use to suggest misconduct.

He alleged the photo was supplied by former Labor councillor and lawyer for fugitive developer Mr Nassif, Sharangan Maheswaran.

Mr Elliott rejected the allegations, previously telling Nine Newspapers he looked forward to the possibility of providing his "own observations".

In an intercepted phone call, Mr Nassif said of Ms Petinos: "She's 'gonna be my girl." (AAP: Bianca De Marchi)

On Friday, Shadow Jobs and Industry Minister Eleni Petinos will become the second Liberal frontbencher to give evidence.

Ms Petinos is not accused of any wrongdoing.

An intercepted phone call played earlier in the inquiry suggested Mr Nassif believed she would replace then-fair trading minister Kevin Anderson in a cabinet reshuffle.

"I'm gonna step on his neck and strip him from his job," Mr Nassif said.

"Just give me two months, because the consumer affairs minister, she's 'gonna be my girl, and the fair-trading minister, she's 'gonna be one of my girls too."

Two months later, Ms Petinos replaced Mr Anderson in the reshuffle.

Former NSW building commissioner David Chandler resigned in 2022 following an investigation commissioned by Ms Petinos's office, but that was later reversed and he remained in the role until 2024.

title: NRLW's Roosters fly against Broncos amid controversy
text:
The Sydney Roosters have strengthened their grip on a second consecutive NRLW minor premiership by enacting a modicum of grand final revenge in a 34-20 victory against Brisbane.

In a stirring rematch of last year's decider, in which the Broncos triumphed, it was the Roosters' sparkling attack that proved the difference at Lang Park on Saturday.

However, the game was overshadowed by a controversial bunker decision to award Roosters winger Brydie Parker a try despite her teammate Jess Sergis pushing Broncos centre Deleni Paitai in the back in the lead-up to the 35th-minute score.

The Tricolours added another three unanswered four-pointers to their tally while prop Brianna Clark was sent to the sin bin for a dangerous tackle.

Although Ali Brigginshaw's stand-in Georgia Bartlett closed the deficit in the 56th minute, Parker brought up her hat-trick, and Sergis crossed again to keep the Roosters (7-0) undefeated.

After suffering its worst loss in club history to Canberra last round, Brisbane started hot by finding two of the first three tries through a speedy Tamika Upton and interchange Chelsea Lenarduzzi.

But on the stroke of half-time, a potential Broncos penalty try wasn't awarded despite winger Kerri Johnson getting tackled in the air centimetres from the line.

The Roosters, however, surged home to keep their one-win advantage on top of the ladder with four games to play.

Eels earn first win as Bulldogs suffer pair of sin-bins

At Western Sydney Stadium, a pair of damaging sin-binnings helped Parramatta end its winless start to the season as it weathered a willing Canterbury comeback to win 30-18.

Having lost their opening six games of the campaign, the Eels started fast as hooker Taneka Todhunter and halfback Rachael Pearson crashed over after Canterbury interchange Latisha Smythe was binned.

Even after the 22-year-old returned, both second-rower Mahalia Murphy and five-eighth Cassey Tohi-Hiku crossed to help Parramatta to a 22-0 half-time lead.

The Bulldogs thrust themselves into the contest when centre Monica Tagoai charged onto a pinpoint kick from Tayla Preston before substitute Evelyn Roberts and prop Alexis Tauaneai snared four-pointers.

But a second sin-bin to back-rower Tamika Jones for a hip-drop tackle proved costly as fullback Abbi Church went on a 95-metre tear to complete the victory.

Titans continue hot streak with sixth win in a row

Gold Coast claimed a sixth-consecutive win for the first time in the club's history and moved into second place, as they staved off St George Illawarra 26-10 at Robina Stadium.

Celebrating their 50th NRLW match, the Titans charged out of the gates, scoring three unanswered tries, but winger Maria Paseka stormed over to reduce the home team's lead to 14-4 at the break.

Prop Ruby-Jean Kennard-Ellis gave the Dragons hope of a major boilover, although Gold Coast flicked a switch, and a classy kick-and-chase by sevens convert Teagan Levi before a try to second-rower Evania Isa'ako sealed the victory.

title: Victorian farmers welcome rain ahead of expected dry summer
text:
As some sunshine and clear skies begin to emerge across Victoria, many farmers across the state are both rejoicing and ruing recent heavy rainfall.

Some growers in western Victoria have lost up to 15 per cent of their crops, while others have turned to drones to spray crops in inaccessible paddocks after up to 150 millimetres of rain fell across the state and caused flooding last week.

But despite the wet conditions, spirits remain high, with the critical spring months ahead and the forecast El Niño weather pattern in spring and summer predicted to be one of the strongest on record.

Broadacre cropping farmer Russell Hocking has lost about 15 per cent of his crop to flooding.

He predicted he could lose a further 10 per cent of his crop, which is visibly waterlogged, if the paddocks do not dry up soon.

Operating across two properties at Prairie, north of Bendigo, and Werrimull, west of Mildura, Mr Hocking said he had experienced the good and the bad of the recent rain.

"The whole Mallee looks excellent, but our farm at Prairie is extremely wet," he said.

"The barley's pretty sick, lentils are very sick, the wheat and oats look okay.

" We're just sneaking by at the minute, but we're hopeful of a sunny, dry couple of weeks ahead. "

Both properties have already exceeded their average annual rainfall, with the Prairie farm getting 410mm so far this year, and Werrimull receiving 348mm.

An aerial photo taken on July 9 shows extensive flooding around Russell Hocking's Prairie property. (Supplied: Russell Hocking)

Both properties headed into sowing with more than 200mm of rain for the year.

By July, the conditions at Prairie had taken a turn for the worse.

A four-day deluge dumped 80mm on the property at the end of June and start of July and resulted in widespread flooding of low-lying crops.

In the past week, Prairie has received close to 40mm, while the farm at Werrimull had 25-30mm in the same rain event.

About 15 per cent of crops on Russell Hocking's Prairie farm have been lost. (Supplied: Russell Hocking)

However, Mr Hocking said he was "still quite positive" about the season, with a full profile of moisture heading into spring.

"The farm at Werrimull, I'd say barring a frost, it's hard to see things not being average, above or even well above average," Mr Hocking said.

Wet paddocks force aerial spraying

Agronomise farm consultant Simon Craig said the wet conditions had increased disease pressure, and a heightened demand for fungicide was resulting in supply shortages.

"Certainly, the rain has increased demand, and growers are probably going to have to be a little bit more open to looking at different chemical products," Mr Craig said.

He said the lack of availability was forcing growers to "think outside the box" to stay on top of disease.

He said growers needed to act now.

"A lot of the fungicide products we require in those crop types are protectants, so they've got to be applied before the disease appears in the crop," he said.

Simon Craig says growers have had to think outside the box to manage disease risk. (Supplied: Simon Craig)

Mr Craig said growers had to find a way to spray their paddocks or risk serious yield losses.

"There's a few other options now than what there was many years ago, like drone and helicopter spraying," he said.

Price-wise, Mr Craig said aerial spraying was more than double the cost of tractor spraying.

"You're looking at probably $8-$10 a hectare doing a contractor boom spray," he said.

"However, with a plane, you're probably looking anywhere between $24-$26 a hectare."

On the waiting list

South-west Victorian dairy farmer Craig Dwyer said he was on the waiting list for aerial spraying on his property at Bullaharre.

"We've had to get ourselves in the queue for the chopper, which I think is arriving midweek to put out our next batch of fertiliser," Mr Dwyer said.

" It's just too wet to traffic paddocks at the moment. "

Mr Dwyer said the property had almost reached its threshold for water, but after two years of drought, all rain was welcome.

"I don't think you'll ever hear me say the words, 'It's far too wet,'" he said.

'The dams are full'

In north-east Victoria, Lima East cattle farmer Damien Gerrans received just under 100mm last weekend.

"The dams are full and the creeks have burst their banks," Mr Gerrans said.

"It's the biggest rain event we've had in a while but the season has been great so far.

"We're still watching the long-range forecast for an early and dry summer, but this sets us up well.

The rain has flooded Mr Gerrans's low-lying country, and he has had to move his herd to higher ground.

"If they were still down on the flats they would be knee deep [in water]."

NationalNSWCity life No meal, no drink: Regulator blocks Boathouse’s bid to loosen liquor rules at popular Sydney beach David Barwell August 16, 2026 — 11:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A plan by one of Sydney’s best-known waterfront venues to loosen its liquor restrictions has been sunk by the state’s licensing regulator after a wave of community opposition over noise, alcohol-related harm and impacts on wildlife. The NSW Independent Liquor & Gaming Authority has refused an application by The Boathouse at Shelly Beach in Manly for a primary service authorisation – a licensing change that would have allowed patrons to buy alcohol without also being legally required to order a full meal. Julie Meldrum (right) and Merrilee Linear from Sydney Wildlife Rescue led objections to The Boathouse at Shelly Beach wanting to serve alcohol without patrons needing to buy food. James Brickwood The Boathouse Group, in its application to ILGA, said the change would have allowed patrons greater flexibility to meet friends, drop in after work or take in the ocean views over a drink. The venue said the change was also in line with the NSW government’s recently enacted “vibrancy reforms”, designed to remove unnecessary licensing restrictions and red tape facing the hospitality industry.

Advertisement

But the proposal sparked intense opposition from locals and environmental advocates, with ILGA receiving 114 formal objections during the public consultation process. Opponents raised concerns about potential late-night antisocial behaviour, “binge-drinking”, traffic congestion, noise disturbances affecting nearby homes and impacts on nearby nesting grounds for native birdlife. The Boathouse restaurant overlooking Shelly Beach in Manly. James Brickwood The National Parks Association of NSW also lodged a formal objection due potential impacts on the venue’s “sensitive coastal and environmental setting”. The public pushback prompted Boathouse Group chief executive Antony Jones to write directly to residents during the assessment process, insisting the proposal was not designed to turn the restaurant into a “nightclub” and would have involved maintaining the venue’s existing trading hours, which run to midnight from Monday to Saturday and 10pm on Sundays.

Advertisement

A Boathouse spokesman claimed opposition had been fuelled by a campaign led by resident group Marine Parade Action Alliance, which the company said had portrayed the application as an attempt to extend trading hours and turn the venue into a late-night drinking destination. “Neither was true,” the spokesman said. But Marine Parade Action Alliance co-founder Julie Meldrum said the group had heard from hundreds of residents concerned about the potential effects on the environment, community safety and neighbourhood amenity. “By not providing food with drinks, it increases the risk of intoxication and antisocial behaviour in an area very close to people’s homes,” she said. “Shelly Beach is a natural wide open area which means noise would have been amplified and the impact on the environment would have been extraordinary.

Advertisement

“It’s also a no-alcohol zone, so it’s quite extraordinary that it was even being considered in the first place.” Related Article City life Sydney gardener fined over destruction of 287 foreshore trees In refusing the application, ILGA chair Caroline Lamb noted the proposal had generated a “significant number” of objections and concluded it risked causing “detriment to the local community”. Lamb also cited higher-than-average rates of alcohol-related assaults across Manly, as well as the concentration of licensed venues in the area. “On balance, (ILGA is) not satisfied that the proposal is in the public interest,” she wrote.

Advertisement

The Boathouse Group said it was disappointed by the decision, noting that neither NSW Police nor Northern Beaches Council had objected to the application. “What we were seeking was an authorisation appropriate to a quality food-led venue in a relatively secluded location – not to add to the concentration of late-night drinking establishments,” the spokesman said. The company also challenged ILGA’s reliance on suburb-wide crime statistics, arguing the venue had not been subject to any liquor enforcement action during the last five years and was not located in a crime hotspot. Cambridge, England — When Cambridge University interviewed Jason Arday for one of the most prestigious sociology positions in the world, he was an early career scholar and underqualified, by the school’s own standards. Cambridge’s requirements, reviewed by The New York Times, called for “an outstanding research record of international stature” and a “proven successful track record” supervising doctorate students. Arday had a modest publication record and had bounced from one university to the next — not staying long enough to oversee a full three-year-or-more doctorate. At 37, Jason Arday became the youngest black professor at the University of Cambridge in its history. Cambridge hired him anyway in 2023, making him, at 37, the university’s youngest black professor at a time when the school was under pressure to diversify. In doing so, Cambridge thrust him into the international limelight, giving him a platform at one of the world’s elite universities to champion academic diversity and making him a target for critics. Arday was found dead in London on Friday, days after resigning his job amid accusations that he had plagiarised chunks of his papers, embellished parts of his recently published memoir and fabricated aspects of his life story. The controversy exploded along cultural fault lines — race, neurodiversity and academic hiring. In his August 5 resignation letter, he wrote, “I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgment.” He added, “This is not the end of my work. It is simply the end of this chapter.” His family said that, since starting at Cambridge, Arday had faced a campaign of scrutiny intended to undermine him. That became too much for him, they said.

Advertisement

Questions about Arday’s career are unlikely to end with his death, however, because they were as much about Cambridge as they were about him. The centuries-old alma mater of Isaac Newton, William Wordsworth and kings and queens, Cambridge now faces deep scrutiny about its decision-making, even from its own faculty. Too good to be true While Arday was underqualified for his job, he had a remarkable story: a tale of being diagnosed early with autism and having such significant developmental delays that he spent his entire childhood in a special-needs school. In his account, he did not speak until age 11 or read until 18, yet he managed to earn his doctorate and begin giving keynote speeches on the academic circuit. Also, he had run 30 marathons in 35 days for charity, a feat that would have placed him among the world’s elite athletes. King’s College, Cambridge. Supporters say Jason Arday is a victim of racially motivated attacks. Bloomberg If, in hindsight, elements of Arday’s story seemed too good to be true, Cambridge ignored repeated warning signs. A review of internal Cambridge documents and interviews with former colleagues and associates shows that, in addition to passing over more experienced candidates for the job, administrators gushed publicly about Arday’s scholarship and privately disregarded complaints about his work. They declined to investigate plagiarism concerns and accused his critics of a “vile campaign” to discredit him.

Advertisement

Arday’s claims about not speaking were false, a former classmate and a speech professional who worked with him told the Times. His supposedly remarkable trajectory from non-verbal preteen to PhD had no precedent in medical literature, experts in developmental and speech delays say. That should have set off alarm bells for the Cambridge hiring committee, which included a child psychiatrist who had done research on autism, experts said. ‘DEI Kool-Aid’ Before Arday’s death, conservative commentators seized on his fall as evidence of diversity-and-inclusion efforts run amok. They said that Cambridge had been so eager to diversify that administrators let their judgment be clouded. Related Article Diversity Diversity programs ‘must die’: Trump pushback gathers pace in Australia “They seem to have drunk the DEI Kool-Aid,” Jacob Rees-Mogg, a former Conservative lawmaker in Britain, said early this past week on The Telegraph’s “Daily T” podcast. Prominent academics on the left agree that Cambridge must answer for its decisions. They say the ordeal has fuelled racism and cast unjustified aspersions on accomplished scholars of colour.

Advertisement

Cambridge said on Friday that it was “desperately saddened” to hear of Arday’s death. An administrator, in a letter to the faculty on Tuesday, called the misconduct accusations “an aberration” and “troubling”. A spokesperson separately declined to answer a list of questions about his hiring and his time there, citing a planned independent investigation — a difficult inquiry that will likely be made even more uncomfortable following Arday’s death. Arday, for his part, had worked hard to silence any questioning of his credentials. When a journalist for Times Higher Education, a respected academic industry publication, asked about plagiarism last year, a prominent British defamation law firm had helped kill the article, the journalist said. Arday later reported the journalist to the police. When a scholar from another university questioned his work, Arday turned the tables and filed a racism complaint with the other school, according to someone with direct knowledge of the complaint. That person, like some others who spoke to the Times, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid being dragged publicly into the controversy. Arday never squarely addressed the questions of plagiarism and fabrication. But what is clear from interviews and public records is that elements of the story would have been easy for Cambridge to check. ‘It just stretches credulity’ Arday, the child of Ghanaian immigrants, grew up in public housing in an ethnically mixed, working-class quarter of South London. Early on, he was identified as having learning difficulties.

Advertisement

Arday has claimed that before age 11, he could understand language but not speak. In 2022, before interviewing with Cambridge, he said that he had been educated exclusively in a special-needs school “with other pupils that had very severe learning difficulties and physical disabilities”. Jason Arday was Cambridge University’s youngest black professor. Joe Giddens/PA via AP In his memoir, published on Tuesday, he gave a different account, saying he attended a mainstream school but spent time sequestered alone in a classroom, again without speaking. Both tales are false, according to people who knew Arday as a child and spoke with the Times before his death. A speech professional who worked closely with the young Arday recalled him having a language delay but speaking with both children and adults. One former schoolmate, Jonathan Stewart, recalled Arday cracking jokes and putting on playful accents in a minivan on the way to church activities as children. While non-verbal children could certainly learn to speak, even at a late age, the rapid development described by Arday had no precedent in clinical literature, three experts on autism and speech said.

title: The surprising story behind Fiji's deep ties to Israel
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Long ago, the story goes, a great double-hulled canoe called the Kaunitoni came from the west, carrying the first ancestral chiefs of the iTaukei (indigenous Fijians). At its head, in one version of the tradition, stood their leader, Lutunasobasoba.

The voyagers had come a seemingly impossible distance: from Thebes in ancient Egypt — earlier still, some say, from a place farther west, via Israel — down the Nile to Lake Tanganyika, across the Indian Ocean, and finally to Vuda, on the western coast of Viti Levu, Fiji's largest island.

Somewhere in that crossing, a sacred box went over the side.

In some tellings, it carried the written record of the people's laws and genealogies — lost, like the canoe's other cargo, somewhere in the churning sea.

For most of the past century, this has been one of the best-known versions of Fiji's national origin story. The mission schools taught it; so did the primary schools. Radio carried it further still, until it became part of the way generations of Fijians understood their ancestry.
