title: Star professor’s death leaves Cambridge exposed to hard questions on race and hiring
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cambridge, England — When Cambridge University interviewed Jason Arday for one of the most prestigious sociology positions in the world, he was an early career scholar and underqualified, by the school’s own standards. Cambridge’s requirements, reviewed by The New York Times, called for “an outstanding research record of international stature” and a “proven successful track record” supervising doctorate students. Arday had a modest publication record and had bounced from one university to the next — not staying long enough to oversee a full three-year-or-more doctorate. At 37, Jason Arday became the youngest black professor at the University of Cambridge in its history. Cambridge hired him anyway in 2023, making him, at 37, the university’s youngest black professor at a time when the school was under pressure to diversify. In doing so, Cambridge thrust him into the international limelight, giving him a platform at one of the world’s elite universities to champion academic diversity and making him a target for critics. Arday was found dead in London on Friday, days after resigning his job amid accusations that he had plagiarised chunks of his papers, embellished parts of his recently published memoir and fabricated aspects of his life story. The controversy exploded along cultural fault lines — race, neurodiversity and academic hiring. In his August 5 resignation letter, he wrote, “I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgment.” He added, “This is not the end of my work. It is simply the end of this chapter.” His family said that, since starting at Cambridge, Arday had faced a campaign of scrutiny intended to undermine him. That became too much for him, they said.

Advertisement

Questions about Arday’s career are unlikely to end with his death, however, because they were as much about Cambridge as they were about him. The centuries-old alma mater of Isaac Newton, William Wordsworth and kings and queens, Cambridge now faces deep scrutiny about its decision-making, even from its own faculty. Too good to be true While Arday was underqualified for his job, he had a remarkable story: a tale of being diagnosed early with autism and having such significant developmental delays that he spent his entire childhood in a special-needs school. In his account, he did not speak until age 11 or read until 18, yet he managed to earn his doctorate and begin giving keynote speeches on the academic circuit. Also, he had run 30 marathons in 35 days for charity, a feat that would have placed him among the world’s elite athletes. King’s College, Cambridge. Supporters say Jason Arday is a victim of racially motivated attacks. Bloomberg If, in hindsight, elements of Arday’s story seemed too good to be true, Cambridge ignored repeated warning signs. A review of internal Cambridge documents and interviews with former colleagues and associates shows that, in addition to passing over more experienced candidates for the job, administrators gushed publicly about Arday’s scholarship and privately disregarded complaints about his work. They declined to investigate plagiarism concerns and accused his critics of a “vile campaign” to discredit him.

Advertisement

Arday’s claims about not speaking were false, a former classmate and a speech professional who worked with him told the Times. His supposedly remarkable trajectory from non-verbal preteen to PhD had no precedent in medical literature, experts in developmental and speech delays say. That should have set off alarm bells for the Cambridge hiring committee, which included a child psychiatrist who had done research on autism, experts said. ‘DEI Kool-Aid’ Before Arday’s death, conservative commentators seized on his fall as evidence of diversity-and-inclusion efforts run amok. They said that Cambridge had been so eager to diversify that administrators let their judgment be clouded. Related Article Diversity Diversity programs ‘must die’: Trump pushback gathers pace in Australia “They seem to have drunk the DEI Kool-Aid,” Jacob Rees-Mogg, a former Conservative lawmaker in Britain, said early this past week on The Telegraph’s “Daily T” podcast. Prominent academics on the left agree that Cambridge must answer for its decisions. They say the ordeal has fuelled racism and cast unjustified aspersions on accomplished scholars of colour.

Advertisement

Cambridge said on Friday that it was “desperately saddened” to hear of Arday’s death. An administrator, in a letter to the faculty on Tuesday, called the misconduct accusations “an aberration” and “troubling”. A spokesperson separately declined to answer a list of questions about his hiring and his time there, citing a planned independent investigation — a difficult inquiry that will likely be made even more uncomfortable following Arday’s death. Arday, for his part, had worked hard to silence any questioning of his credentials. When a journalist for Times Higher Education, a respected academic industry publication, asked about plagiarism last year, a prominent British defamation law firm had helped kill the article, the journalist said. Arday later reported the journalist to the police. When a scholar from another university questioned his work, Arday turned the tables and filed a racism complaint with the other school, according to someone with direct knowledge of the complaint. That person, like some others who spoke to the Times, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid being dragged publicly into the controversy. Arday never squarely addressed the questions of plagiarism and fabrication. But what is clear from interviews and public records is that elements of the story would have been easy for Cambridge to check. ‘It just stretches credulity’ Arday, the child of Ghanaian immigrants, grew up in public housing in an ethnically mixed, working-class quarter of South London. Early on, he was identified as having learning difficulties.

Advertisement

Arday has claimed that before age 11, he could understand language but not speak. In 2022, before interviewing with Cambridge, he said that he had been educated exclusively in a special-needs school “with other pupils that had very severe learning difficulties and physical disabilities”. Jason Arday was Cambridge University’s youngest black professor. Joe Giddens/PA via AP In his memoir, published on Tuesday, he gave a different account, saying he attended a mainstream school but spent time sequestered alone in a classroom, again without speaking. Both tales are false, according to people who knew Arday as a child and spoke with the Times before his death. A speech professional who worked closely with the young Arday recalled him having a language delay but speaking with both children and adults. One former schoolmate, Jonathan Stewart, recalled Arday cracking jokes and putting on playful accents in a minivan on the way to church activities as children. While non-verbal children could certainly learn to speak, even at a late age, the rapid development described by Arday had no precedent in clinical literature, three experts on autism and speech said.

title: Pauline Hanson breaks silence on ‘gayest party’ claim

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has stood by comments she made 30 years ago condemning the Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras while responding to colleague Barnaby Joyce's claim they have "one of the gayest parties in Australia".

Senator Hanson did not back Mr Joyce's claim when asked about it on Sunday, saying that "that's Barnaby, and Barnaby is Barnaby".

"I know there are gay people that work for One Nation ... and good on them," she told News24.

"They got it on their merit, not because of their sexuality or ... their preference.

"It's none of my business and I don't care."

Mr Joyce made the comment while being asked about homophobic remarks from a former One Nation candidate in last year's West Australian state election.

Parminder Singh, who failed to win an upper house seat, called homosexuality a "mental illness" that he blamed "on the parents because parents are too busy" in a podcast appearance.

Mr Singh this week apologised, saying he was "sorry I hurt people".

Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras participants made an effigy of Pauline Hanson in 1997. Picture: News Corp Australia

"I was repeating something I had heard people saying on social media about homosexuality being a mental illness," he said.

"I should not have presented that as a fact. I respect everyone, and I believe every person in Australia should be free to live their life with dignity, equality and respect."

﻿'I still don't like the gay Mardi Gras'

During her Sunday interview, Senator Hanson was also asked about comments about Mardi Gras that she made during an interview in 1996.

"I don't like it because it's promoting something ... that is not natural," she said at the time.

Asked if she still held that view, she said "the world has changed" and noted that Australia had since legalised same-sex marriage.

"Now that's acceptable, and I've got no problem with it," Senator Hanson said, adding that "people can do what they want in their life".

The Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras is worth almost $40m to the NSW economy. Picture: NewsWire / Ben Symons

Asked why, Senator Hanson could not say.

"That's my opinion," she said.

Pressed further, she said: "I just don't like the gay Mardi Gras."

She went on to say that "your own personal sexuality should be kept ... behind closed doors".

"It's no one's business to do it out there with the gay Mardi Gras," she said.

The Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras is the country's biggest LGBTQ+ festival and one of the largest in the world.

It draws tens of thousands of visitors to Sydney and pumps almost $40m into NSW's economy.

title: ‘Open your eyes’: Horror snow season reality
text:
If Jackson Harvey has any childhood memories not directly tied to the depths of winter, you'll be hard pressed to coax them out of him.

Raised in the mountains of Colorado by an American dad and an Aussie mum, the 23-year-old Olympic moguls skier grew up surrounded by great big piles of snow – a childhood experience he fears may soon become extinct, as global warming lashes Australia's alpine communities.

Jackson Harvey represented Australia at the Winter Olympics in Italy earlier this year. Picture: Supplied / Chris Hocking

"I remember there would always be this sense of anticipation when you knew you and your friends would be going out skiing the next day. They'd just be these endless days of skiing powder and just enjoying everybody's company," Harvey said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"That's what really sparked my love for the mountains and winter."

Working alongside a coalition of scientists and winter athletes called Protect Our Winters (POW), Harvey has just spent a week in Canberra calling on politicians to support a national alpine resistance plan.

He moved to Australia in 2023 to join the Olympic moguls skiing team, but as a teenager he spent the 2015 ski season in Jindabyne on exchange at the local Central School.

"One of my most vivid memories of that season was training on the famous Toppa's Dream mogul course at Perisher Resort, which is this behemoth of a course. It's known for its steep pitch, and it's quite robust," Harvey said.

Harvey is studying environmental science at Griffith University, doubling the level of his involvement in protecting alpine communities. Picture: Supplied

He has joined Protect Our Winters as an athlete ambassador. Picture: supplied / Chris Hocking

"When I moved out to join the national team, we would train on the same course. For the last four years now, the main domestic moguls skiing event, which is held on Toppa's Dream, has been shortened because of extreme weather circumstances like rain and high wind.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The snow deteriorates so much that the jumps fall apart and the conditions become too unsafe and unsustainable to hold the event."

The average temperature in the Australian Alps has risen by about 2C since the middle of the 20th century, and while that may not sound like much, the variation has caused a 30 per cent reduction in snow cover.

The changes are causing significant stress for local communities who have been forced to endure shortened snow seasons and, therefore, less profitability during key tourist influx periods.

The 2026 snow season has been characterised by patchy coverage, above-average temperatures and rainfall washing away large clumps of snow. Picture: supplied

Winter sports commentator and international freeskier Mia Rennie – "Miff" to her mates – was raised in Cabramurra on the western side of the Snowy Mountains, the town where local average temperatures are recorded each year.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

She said. winters experienced by locals and tourists today are a far cry from the snow seasons of her childhood.

"During the winter, we used to regularly have to dig our door out of the snow, it was quite common. Now, when you tell kids that used to happen in Australia, it feels like a foreign story – they can't relate to it," she said.

"I used to ski at Selwyn Snow Resort when my parents were ski patrollers there, and the change has been so drastic. After the 2019 fires, they burned down and were forced to rebuild … but they can't even hold ski seasons anymore.

"The lodge owners are really struggling this year to make the money. They're losing customers, and it's a lot quieter around town, especially Selwyn and Cabramurra.

Mia Rennie grew up on the NSW South Coast but spent most winter holidays on the ski slopes, honing her craft. Picture: Supplied / Protect Our Winters

"They just don't get the snowfall they need … it's a scary, daunting thing. I had my first turns there as a kid, and I know my kids won't."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Rennie said part of the reason she went to Canberra this week was to make sure everybody was "on the same page" about how dire the situation was.

"This isn't something anybody can deny. The facts are there," she said.

"People need to open their eyes and see that our winters have been shortening, snowfall is less and it's decreasing every year. Nothing can be denied anymore."

Climate scientist and lead author of the National Climate Risk Assessment Andrew Watkins said one of the major issues caused by the rise in temperature was snow now falling as rain.

The Protect Our Winters team spoke to politicians while in Canberra, including former pro winter athlete and independent MP Zali Steggall. Picture: Protect Our Winters

"Typically, a ski season has between three and five big snowfall events, but unfortunately as we've seen this season, some of those events are falling as rain, which is the natural enemy of snow," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The future of drier and warmer conditions is really concerning."

Dr Watkins said the flow-on effects could be even more devastating, citing issues around water flow and Indigenous heritage

"There's a huge range of aspects well beyond just the environment and skiers. It's not even just the communities on top of the mountain, it's agriculture too," he said.

"Around 29 per cent of the water that comes into the Murray Darling Basin comes from the high country.

"There's First Nations aspects as well. This place has been part of their culture for tens of thousands of years. Ultimately, all of these things are at risk."

Andrew Watkins said he and his mates wouldn't even drive up to the mountains if less than a metre of snow had fallen back in the '90s. Picture: Supplied

Ruby Olsson co-authored a report detailing the impacts of climate change on the Australian Alps' famous snow gum trees. Picture: Supplied

According to Dr Watkins, there is a glaring need for a "co-ordinated mechanism" between state and federal governments to keep alpine communities thriving.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"At the moment, some pieces of the adaptation process are all over the place," he said.

"There's nothing really co-ordinating it together and there's nothing at the moment really collecting all the voices.

"We're asking the government to form a plan that doesn't leave anybody behind."

Social scientist Ruby Olsson believes a national alpine adaptation plan is the key to keeping Australia's alpine regions safe.

Dr Watkins is a diehard winter sportsman. Picture: Supplied

"There is actually quite a lot of adaptation happening in the Alps, but it's happening at a very disjointed, fragmented, individual level," she said.

"There's this missed opportunity to have something multi-jurisdictional, so across NSW, Victoria and the ACT. There's also a role for private landowners to get involved, and on top of all of this we're hoping the commonwealth can take on a co-ordinating role."

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Other defined areas of extreme environmental significance, like the Great Barrier Reef, are governed by plans similar to the one POW is advocating for.

Harvey believes it is our responsibility to look after the environment on behalf of future generations. Picture: Supplied

Harvey said the best way to think about the situation was to assume we were "borrowing the environment from our children and grandchildren".

"We want to leave it in a really good place for them, and that's our responsibility. There's a great deal of urgency here," he said.

"My job in Canberra is not to ask for sympathy as an elite athlete but rather to advocate on behalf of future generations of athletes who deserve their fair shot at the gold medal.

"Everybody deserves to be able to experience the magic of the alpine region. That's what we're here for."
